messages.content: I want to develop selective language-model unlearning: remove information specific to a source while preserving facts that also have independent support, even when those facts appear in the source being removed. Can you help me state the goal precisely?

The goal is to make the removal selective rather than treating everything present in the source as something to forget. Information specific to the removed source should no longer be recoverable in the relevant sense, while facts shared with that source and independently supported should remain usable. The two requirements make that distinction measurable: adaptive source-exclusive extraction success must stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source, and accuracy on independently supported shared facts must drop by at most 2 percentage points versus the original model.
Why distinguish source-exclusive information from facts that merely appear in the source?

Appearing in the source is not, by itself, the same as depending on that source. A fact can occur there and also have independent support. The goal is to remove what is specific to the source without unnecessarily removing those independently supported facts. That is the sense in which the unlearning is selective.
So the aim is not to make the model deny every fact mentioned in the removed source?

Right. That would be broader than the stated goal. If a fact is shared with the removed source but independently supported, preserving accuracy on it is part of the objective. The target of removal is source-specific information, not all content that happens to overlap with the source.
What does the retraining comparison tell us?

It provides the comparison for adaptive attempts to extract source-exclusive information. The requirement is that extraction success for the unlearned model stay within 2 percentage points of extraction success for a model retrained without the source. It is a comparison with that retraining baseline, not a claim that extraction success must be zero or that retraining produces any particular result.
And the original model is the comparison for the shared facts instead?

Yes. For independently supported shared facts, the requirement concerns the drop in accuracy relative to the original model: that drop must be no more than 2 percentage points. The two comparisons serve different purposes. Retraining without the source is the reference for source-exclusive extraction; the original model is the reference for preserving shared-fact accuracy.
Could you clarify the wording around the two 2-percentage-point limits?

For extraction success, “within 2 percentage points” describes how close it must remain to the retraining-without-the-source result. For shared-fact accuracy, “drops at most 2 percentage points” limits how much lower it may be than the original model’s accuracy. Both limits are expressed in percentage points, not as a 2 percent relative change.
Does the shared-fact requirement say the unlearned model has to match the original exactly?

No. It permits an accuracy drop of up to 2 percentage points on independently supported shared facts. The intent is to preserve performance closely, but the stated threshold is not exact equality. Nor does it give an absolute accuracy target independent of the original model.
What is the significance of calling the extraction test adaptive?

It makes clear that the source-exclusive extraction requirement concerns adaptive extraction attempts, rather than only a fixed, unchanging request. The node does not specify a particular procedure for those attempts. Its stated condition is the resulting success comparison: within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source.
I want to be careful not to treat independent support as proof that every shared fact is correct. Is that distinction relevant?

Yes. Here, independent support distinguishes facts that are not supported solely by the source being removed. The requirement is framed in terms of accuracy on those independently supported shared facts; it does not say that mere repetition in another place automatically establishes correctness. The important distinction for this goal is whether removing the source should also erase a fact that has support independent of it.
Would satisfying only the extraction limit meet the goal?

Not by itself. Extraction success could be close to retraining without the source while accuracy on independently supported shared facts falls too far. The goal includes both constraints: limiting recovery of source-exclusive information and keeping the shared-fact accuracy drop to at most 2 percentage points versus the original model.
And high shared-fact accuracy alone would not establish selective unlearning either?

Correct. Preserving shared facts addresses one side of the goal, but source-specific information might still be extractable. The adaptive source-exclusive extraction comparison is the other side. Selectivity requires attending to both rather than treating either measure as a substitute for the other.
Can you say the objective in one concise statement without losing the separate baselines?

Develop language-model unlearning that removes source-specific information while preserving facts independently supported outside the removed source: adaptive source-exclusive extraction success should be within 2 percentage points of retraining without that source, and accuracy on independently supported shared facts should drop no more than 2 percentage points relative to the original model.
Does that statement claim those thresholds have already been achieved?

No. It states the goal and its requirements, not an experimental result. Whether a particular approach meets either threshold would have to be established separately; nothing in the goal alone says that it has.
How might we pursue that selective unlearning goal without treating every fact in the removed source alike?

A proposed approach is to use provenance-linked fact clusters to guide two different operations: gradient ascent on source-exclusive spans, and original-model distillation on independently corroborated facts. The clusters provide the distinction the approach needs—what is specific to the source versus what also has independent corroboration—so that removal and preservation are directed at different content.
What work is the provenance link doing in that proposal?

It connects a fact cluster to the sources relevant to it. Conceptually, that lets the approach distinguish content tied exclusively to the source being removed from facts that also have corroboration independent of that source. The proposal does not specify how those links or clusters are constructed; it says they guide which of the two operations applies.
Why describe them as fact clusters rather than just a list of text passages?

The emphasis is on the underlying facts and their provenance, not merely on whether a particular string occurs in the removed source. A fact shared across sources may be expressed differently in each. Calling them provenance-linked fact clusters conveys that the source relationship matters when deciding what to discourage and what to preserve, without committing to a particular clustering method.
Explain the gradient-ascent side in this context.

The proposed gradient ascent is directed at source-exclusive spans. In general terms, applying ascent to those spans pushes against the model’s fit to that source-specific material. Its intended role here is removal. The proposal does not say that ascent is applied indiscriminately to the entire removed source, nor does it specify a particular loss, schedule, or training procedure.
Is a source-exclusive span simply any span taken from the source?

No. “Source-exclusive” is the important qualifier. The proposal separates spans that carry information specific to the source from facts in the source that have independent corroboration. Treating every span from the source as exclusive would erase the distinction the approach is meant to use.
Then what is the original-model distillation meant to do?

It is the preservation side of the proposal. For independently corroborated facts, distillation from the original model aims to retain the model’s behavior on those facts while the source-exclusive spans are targeted for unlearning. The original model serves as the reference for that preservation; the proposal does not say to distill its behavior on the source-exclusive material being removed.
Could the same fact appear in the removed source and still fall on the distillation side?

Yes. If the fact is independently corroborated, its appearance in the removed source does not by itself make the fact source-exclusive. That is precisely why the proposal uses provenance-linked fact clusters: the source relationship, rather than mere presence in a document, guides whether the approach emphasizes preservation or removal.
Would the distillation step be trying to copy everything the original model knows?

That would be broader than the proposal. The stated distillation target is independently corroborated facts. Copying the original model without that distinction could also preserve source-specific information, which is what the other part of the approach is meant to remove.
How should I describe the relationship between the two operations?

They are complementary parts of one selective proposal. Provenance-linked fact clusters guide gradient ascent toward source-exclusive spans and guide original-model distillation toward independently corroborated facts. One operation is aimed at weakening source-specific information; the other is aimed at retaining facts whose support does not depend solely on the removed source.
Does the proposal imply that gradient ascent alone would preserve the shared facts?

No. The proposal explicitly pairs ascent on source-exclusive spans with distillation on independently corroborated facts. That pairing reflects the need to protect the latter while targeting the former. It does not assert that either operation alone would produce the desired selectivity.
What if I say the clusters prove which facts are true?

That would overstate their stated role. They are provenance-linked and guide the distinction between source-exclusive spans and independently corroborated facts. Independent corroboration is relevant to preserving a fact during source removal, but the proposal does not claim that clustering itself proves truth or settles every possible disagreement about a fact.
Does this description specify how much ascent or distillation to use?

No. It identifies the material each operation targets and the role of provenance-linked fact clusters in guiding that choice. It does not give strengths, weights, an order of operations, or other implementation settings. Those details should not be read into the proposal.
And we should not describe it as an achieved unlearning result yet?

Correct. This is a proposed way to pursue selective unlearning, not a report that source-exclusive extraction or shared-fact accuracy has met the goal’s requirements. The proposal explains the intended division of work between removal and preservation; it does not supply measured outcomes.
Give me a compact version that still makes the division clear.

Use provenance-linked fact clusters to distinguish source-exclusive spans from independently corroborated facts. Apply gradient ascent to the source-exclusive spans to target their removal, while using original-model distillation on the independently corroborated facts to support their preservation.
Can provenance-linked clusters actually separate source-exclusive spans from independently supported facts when the same information is paraphrased across sources?

That is the open question. Paraphrased overlap makes surface wording an unreliable guide: two differently worded passages may express the same fact, while similar wording need not establish independent support for a fact. For the proposed distinction to hold, the clusters would need to connect equivalent factual content with its provenance rather than rely only on matching text. Whether they can do that reliably is not established by the proposal itself.
So if wording differs, I should not automatically call the span source-exclusive?

Right. A span can be unique as text without the fact it expresses being exclusive to the source. If that fact has independent support in another wording, the relevant fact belongs on the independently supported side of the distinction. The question is whether the provenance-linked clusters can recognize that relationship despite the paraphrase.
And if wording is similar across sources, does that settle it the other way?

Not necessarily. Similar wording alone does not resolve whether the same fact is independently supported. The provenance matters, as does what the passages actually assert. The open issue is whether the clusters can distinguish independent factual support from overlap that is only superficial or does not establish the same claim.
I'm getting caught between the terms “span” and “fact.” Are they interchangeable here?

No. A span is a piece of source text; a fact is the content at issue. The proposal targets gradient ascent at source-exclusive spans and uses original-model distillation for independently corroborated facts. Paraphrasing exposes why those levels should not be conflated: the same fact might be conveyed by different spans, and a span’s particular wording might be specific to one source even when part of its factual content has independent support.
Does that mean a single span might not fit neatly into one category?

It raises that possibility conceptually. A span can contain wording or content specific to a source while also conveying a fact that has independent support. The question about cluster separation is therefore not answered merely by assigning an entire passage a label based on where it appeared. The supplied proposal does not specify how such a case would be handled.
What would the clusters have to distinguish in that situation?

They would have to preserve the distinction between what the removed source uniquely contributes and what is independently supported, even when those elements appear together or in paraphrased forms. That describes the distinction needed for the proposal, not a claim that the clusters already achieve it or a prescribed way to construct them.
Could I phrase the uncertainty as an alignment problem between paraphrases and provenance?

Yes, as a conceptual description. The clusters would need to align expressions of the same factual content across different wording while retaining where the support comes from. The unresolved part is whether that alignment and provenance distinction are sufficiently reliable to separate source-exclusive spans from independently supported facts.
Would finding a paraphrase elsewhere automatically establish that the fact is independently supported?

No. A paraphrase may show that similar content appears elsewhere, but appearance and independent support are not identical. The question asks about independently supported facts, so the provenance relationship still matters. The clusters cannot answer the intended question solely by finding another formulation of the same words or claim.
Then could something look source-exclusive just because the other support is phrased differently?

Yes, that is one way paraphrased overlap could complicate the distinction. If the clusters fail to associate differently phrased expressions of the same independently supported fact, they could treat that content as exclusive on the basis of its wording. This is a possible failure mode to consider, not an observed outcome.
Is there also a risk in the opposite direction?

Conceptually, yes. If a cluster groups content together because it sounds similar, it might treat source-specific information as independently supported when the other material does not actually corroborate that information. Again, the point is not that this has happened, but that separating the categories requires more than recognizing verbal resemblance.
How does this question relate to the two operations in the proposal?

The operations depend on the separation the clusters provide. Source-exclusive spans are the proposed targets for gradient ascent; independently corroborated facts are the proposed targets for original-model distillation. If paraphrased overlap makes those categories hard to distinguish, it is unclear whether each operation would be guided to the intended content. That is why the question matters to the proposal.
Should the question be read as asking whether paraphrases can ever be recognized at all?

It is narrower and more consequential than that. Recognizing that two expressions are paraphrases is part of it, but the proposed separation also depends on whether the underlying fact has support independent of the removed source. The question is whether provenance-linked clusters can make that combined distinction despite paraphrased overlap.
I don't want to turn this into a claim that the clustering approach succeeds. What is the careful phrasing?

You could ask: “Can provenance-linked fact clusters reliably distinguish source-exclusive spans from independently supported facts when overlapping factual content is expressed through paraphrases?” That keeps it as a question about the proposal’s key distinction, rather than treating the distinction as already demonstrated.
And we shouldn't answer it just by saying that the clusters have provenance links?

Correct. Provenance links express what the clusters are intended to track; they do not, by themselves, establish that paraphrased content has been grouped correctly or that support is genuinely independent. Those are exactly the issues the question leaves open.
Would you say the challenge is that textual exclusivity and factual exclusivity may come apart?

Yes. Textual exclusivity concerns a particular expression appearing in one source, whereas factual exclusivity concerns whether the information it conveys lacks independent support. Paraphrases can make a fact shared even when its wording is not. The clusters are being asked to preserve that distinction, and whether they can do so is the unresolved issue.
So the precise question is about separating information by support, not merely sorting passages by how closely their wording matches?

Exactly. Wording can be evidence of a relationship, but the distinction at stake is source-exclusive information versus independently supported facts. The open question is whether provenance-linked clusters can maintain that distinction when the relevant overlap is paraphrased rather than verbatim.
I want to make a concrete hypothesis about whether provenance-linked clusters can handle paraphrased overlap. How should I state it?

State it as a testable expectation, not a finding: on ParaphraseProvenance-1, provenance-linked clusters achieve at least 95% source-exclusive precision and at least 95% independently supported fact recall despite paraphrases.
What does the source-exclusive precision part mean?

It concerns what the clusters identify as source-exclusive. A threshold of ≥95% precision means that at least 95% of the items identified as source-exclusive should actually be source-exclusive under the evaluation’s criteria. The hypothesis does not, by itself, specify how many of all source-exclusive items the clusters find.
And independently supported fact recall measures a different side of the distinction?

Yes. A threshold of ≥95% independently supported fact recall means that the clusters should identify at least 95% of the independently supported facts covered by the evaluation. It focuses on not overlooking facts with independent support, rather than on the precision of everything identified as independently supported.
Why pair precision for one category with recall for the other?

The pairing makes two particular errors salient. Source-exclusive precision asks whether items selected as exclusive really belong in that category. Independently supported fact recall asks whether facts that should be recognized as independently supported are being found. The hypothesis specifies those two measures; it does not claim that every other measure of cluster quality also reaches 95%.
Does “despite paraphrases” mean the hypothesis is only about exact matches?

No. It makes paraphrased overlap part of the challenge the hypothesis addresses. The expectation is that the stated precision and recall thresholds hold on ParaphraseProvenance-1 even when relevant content is expressed in different words. It does not require every individual paraphrase to be handled perfectly.
Could a cluster pass the precision threshold simply by labeling very little as source-exclusive?

Precision alone would not rule out that possibility. The hypothesis sets a source-exclusive precision threshold, but does not specify source-exclusive recall. Its second threshold—independently supported fact recall—covers a different category and should not be mistaken for a recall requirement on source-exclusive spans.
Likewise, does high independently supported fact recall ensure that every fact called independently supported really has independent support?

Not on its own. Recall concerns how many independently supported facts are found; it does not state the precision of that label. Keeping the two named metrics distinct is important when explaining what the hypothesis would and would not establish.
I don't want the wording to imply that the clusters have already scored ≥95% on either metric.

Then retain explicit hypothesis language, such as “We hypothesize that, on ParaphraseProvenance-1, provenance-linked clusters will achieve ≥95% source-exclusive precision and ≥95% independently supported fact recall despite paraphrases.” That expresses an expected outcome without presenting measurements or a completed evaluation.
Is ParaphraseProvenance-1 the setting for both thresholds?

Yes. Both thresholds are stated for provenance-linked clusters on ParaphraseProvenance-1. The hypothesis does not specify performance on other settings or say that the same values will hold everywhere.
Should I interpret ≥95% as exactly 95%?
No. The symbol means at least 95%. Each named metric would meet its stated threshold at 95% or above. It is not an assertion that either measured value equals 95%.
How does this speak to separating source-exclusive spans from independently supported facts?

It proposes two ways that separation would show up on ParaphraseProvenance-1: classifications of source-exclusive material would be highly precise, and independently supported facts would rarely be missed, according to the respective ≥95% thresholds. Paraphrases matter because wording alone may not reveal which factual content has independent support.
Would meeting these clustering thresholds prove the unlearning approach meets its downstream goal?

No. This hypothesis concerns the provenance-linked clusters’ source-exclusive precision and independently supported fact recall on ParaphraseProvenance-1. It does not report an unlearning result or establish how subsequent model behavior changes. Good separation would be relevant to guiding the proposed operations, but these clustering metrics are not themselves downstream unlearning measurements.
Can I describe this as a claim about provenance rather than just paraphrase recognition?

Yes, provided you keep it as a hypothesis. Recognizing similar meaning across different wording is not sufficient if the clusters cannot also distinguish whether a fact has independent support. The stated expectation is about source-exclusive precision and independently supported fact recall despite paraphrases, so both the factual relationship and the provenance distinction matter.
What if a fact appears in paraphrased form outside the source being removed? Would that automatically decide its label?

Not automatically. Paraphrased appearance and independent support are related questions, not identical ones. The hypothesis is that provenance-linked clusters can achieve the specified metrics while navigating such overlap; it does not declare a rule that any paraphrase elsewhere makes a fact independently supported.
Would it be accurate to say that every source-exclusive span is correctly identified under this hypothesis?

No. The source-exclusive threshold is precision of at least 95%, not perfect classification or source-exclusive recall. Similarly, the independently supported fact threshold is recall of at least 95%, not a guarantee that every independently supported fact is found. Neither metric should be strengthened beyond what the hypothesis states.
Could you give a final formulation that preserves the benchmark, both metrics, and the uncertainty?

Hypothesis: On ParaphraseProvenance-1, provenance-linked clusters achieve ≥95% source-exclusive precision and ≥95% independently supported fact recall despite paraphrases. This is a predicted clustering outcome, not a reported result.
How should we investigate whether provenance-linked clusters can separate source-exclusive material from shared facts despite paraphrased overlap?

The plan is to construct ParaphraseProvenance-1 with annotated paraphrase pairs, cluster claims by entailment and provenance, and then audit exclusive precision and shared-fact recall. That sequence puts the paraphrase challenge into the material being examined, uses both claim relationships and source relationships to form clusters, and checks the two distinctions the clusters are meant to support.
What is the role of the annotated paraphrase pairs?

They make paraphrased overlap explicit in ParaphraseProvenance-1. If two expressions convey overlapping claims without using the same wording, the annotations provide a way to examine whether clustering follows the claims rather than just the words. The plan does not specify the size of the collection or a particular annotation procedure.
Why cluster claims by entailment rather than simply grouping similar-looking sentences?

Entailment concerns what a claim implies, whereas similar-looking sentences may not express the same information. For this question, the relevant relationship is between claims even when their wording differs. The plan therefore names entailment as one basis for clustering; it does not specify a particular entailment model or rule for forming the clusters.
Does entailment alone establish whether something is source-exclusive?

No. Entailment helps relate the content of claims, but exclusivity also depends on provenance: where the relevant support comes from. That is why the plan calls for clustering by both entailment and provenance. A relationship between claims does not, on its own, establish independent support outside the source at issue.
And provenance alone would not handle the paraphrase problem?

Provenance identifies source relationships, but those relationships need to be connected to the claims being expressed. If overlapping claims are phrased differently, simply recording where each span appeared would not necessarily show that they concern the same fact. The proposed clustering brings entailment and provenance together for that reason.
Is the plan to cluster text spans or the claims they express?

It says to cluster claims by entailment and provenance. The distinction matters: an annotated paraphrase pair concerns expressions in text, but the clustering is meant to track their claimed content and its provenance. The plan does not provide a more detailed representation of those claims.
When does the audit happen?

After constructing ParaphraseProvenance-1 and clustering the claims, the plan is to audit exclusive precision and shared-fact recall. Describing that order does not imply that the benchmark has already been constructed, the claims clustered, or either audit completed.
What would the exclusive-precision audit ask?

It would examine the material identified as exclusive and ask how much of that identified material is actually exclusive under the audit’s reference criteria. That is the precision direction: it focuses on the correctness of exclusive identifications, not on whether every exclusive item was found. The plan names the audit but does not provide an observed precision value.
What would shared-fact recall ask instead?

It would ask how many of the shared facts that should be recognized are captured by the clustering. That is a recall question about missed shared facts, rather than a precision question about everything labeled shared. In this context, the shared-fact distinction is important because a fact may overlap with the source being removed while also having support independent of it.
So those two audits look for different kinds of trouble?

Yes. Exclusive precision draws attention to content identified as source-exclusive when it may not be. Shared-fact recall draws attention to shared facts that the clusters fail to recognize. The plan audits both because paraphrased overlap could complicate either side of the separation; it does not assert that either problem has occurred.
Could I say the paraphrase annotations themselves decide which facts have independent support?

That would go beyond the plan. Paraphrase annotations address the relationship between differently worded expressions. Independent support also requires attention to provenance. The stated plan is to use annotated paraphrase pairs and cluster claims by entailment and provenance before auditing the resulting distinction.
Does the plan prescribe a specific way to determine entailment?

No. It specifies entailment as a basis for clustering claims, but not the mechanism for determining entailment. Likewise, it does not spell out the annotation workflow or the detailed audit procedure. Those are not established by this plan statement.
Could we say that a successful cluster must treat every paraphrase as an identical fact?

That would be too strong. Paraphrase pairs motivate looking past wording, but the plan calls for clustering claims by entailment and provenance, not for declaring every differently worded pair identical in all respects. The audit is there to examine whether the resulting clusters make the intended exclusive-versus-shared distinction.
How does this plan answer the concern about paraphrased overlap without assuming the answer in advance?

It creates a setting with annotated paraphrase pairs, applies clustering that considers both claim content and provenance, and then audits exclusive precision and shared-fact recall. Those steps provide a way to examine the concern. They do not presume that the clusters will separate the categories successfully.
Would either audit by itself cover the whole question?

Neither named audit covers both sides on its own. Exclusive precision examines the reliability of exclusive identifications; shared-fact recall examines whether shared facts are being found. Together they address two important aspects of separating the categories, while the plan makes no broader claim that these are every possible measure of clustering quality.
Please put the plan in a single sentence, keeping the order clear.
Construct ParaphraseProvenance-1 with annotated paraphrase pairs, cluster claims by entailment and provenance, then audit exclusive precision and shared-fact recall.
What is the concrete activity for examining the clustering question on ParaphraseProvenance-1?

Annotate 1,200 ParaphraseProvenance-1 claims, run entailment-provenance clustering, and measure exclusive precision and shared-fact recall against blinded labels. Those are the activities to carry out; the description does not report measurements or say the work is complete.
Is 1,200 the number of claims or the number of paraphrase pairs?
It is 1,200 claims. The activity does not give a count of paraphrase pairs, so it would be inaccurate to describe the 1,200 as pairs.
What does annotating the claims contribute?

It makes the ParaphraseProvenance-1 claims available for the stated clustering and measurement activity. The activity names the claims to annotate but does not specify the annotation scheme, who performs the annotation, or how disagreements would be handled.
When you say “run entailment-provenance clustering,” what are the two things it brings together?

Entailment concerns relationships among what the claims assert; provenance concerns their source relationships. Bringing both into the clustering is pertinent when differently worded claims may overlap in content but differ in whether they have support independent of the source at issue. The activity does not specify a clustering algorithm.
Should I describe this as clustering the 1,200 claims by exact wording?

No. The stated activity is entailment-provenance clustering, not exact-word matching. Exact wording alone would not express either the entailment relationship or the provenance distinction named here.
Are the blinded labels what the clusters are built from?

The activity says to measure exclusive precision and shared-fact recall against blinded labels. That identifies the labels as the reference for measurement. It does not say that the clustering is built from those labels, and it does not describe the precise blinding arrangement.
Can you explain that distinction without assuming a particular evaluation setup?

Yes. Running the clustering produces the distinctions to be assessed; measuring against blinded labels compares those distinctions with a labeled reference. Beyond that, the activity does not specify who can see which labels, when they can see them, or how the labels were produced.
What question does exclusive precision answer in this measurement?

It asks, among the material identified as exclusive, how much is exclusive according to the blinded labels. It assesses the reliability of the exclusive identifications. It does not, by itself, say how many exclusive items the clustering missed.
And what is the corresponding question for shared-fact recall?

It asks how much of the shared-fact material represented by the blinded labels is recognized by the clustering. Recall is about finding those shared facts, rather than about whether every item identified as shared is correctly identified.
Does “shared-fact” here mean any claim that appears in the source being removed?

No. In this discussion, the important distinction is whether a fact also has independent support. Mere appearance in the source does not establish that distinction. Measuring shared-fact recall is meant to examine recognition of the shared-fact category, not simply count all claims present in the source.
Why measure both exclusive precision and shared-fact recall?

They examine different sides of the separation. Exclusive precision addresses whether exclusive identifications are warranted; shared-fact recall addresses whether shared facts are overlooked. Using both is especially pertinent to the question of whether paraphrased overlap can be handled without confusing source-specific content with independently supported facts.
Does the activity say that the two measurements will reach any particular values?

No. It directs that they be measured against blinded labels, but it supplies no measured values. We should not describe a result, a pass or fail judgment, or a completed audit on the basis of this activity statement.
Would measuring these clustering properties also tell us how the language model performs after unlearning?

Not on its own. This activity concerns annotating claims, running clustering, and measuring the resulting exclusive precision and shared-fact recall. It does not include a measurement of model behavior after unlearning.
Could I say that the labels are blinded so the clustering cannot use them?

That asserts more about the blinding arrangement than the activity specifies. The careful wording is simply that exclusive precision and shared-fact recall are measured against blinded labels. We can explain their role as the reference for measurement without assigning a specific blinding procedure.
What's the shortest faithful account of the activity?
Annotate 1,200 ParaphraseProvenance-1 claims, run entailment-provenance clustering, then measure exclusive precision and shared-fact recall against blinded labels.
What did the clustering measurements show on ParaphraseProvenance-1?

On 1,200 ParaphraseProvenance-1 claims, clustering achieved 96.1% source-exclusive precision and 95.4% independently supported fact recall. Those are measured clustering results, not measurements of the language model after unlearning.
Can you unpack the 96.1% figure?

It is source-exclusive precision. Among the items the clustering identified as source-exclusive, 96.1% were source-exclusive according to the evaluation. It describes the reliability of that identification, not the fraction of all source-exclusive material that the clustering found.
So it would be wrong to say that 96.1% of the 1,200 claims were source-exclusive?

Yes. The 1,200 is the number of ParaphraseProvenance-1 claims considered. The 96.1% is a precision value, whose denominator is the material identified as source-exclusive—not all 1,200 claims. The result does not state how many claims received that identification.
What does the 95.4% figure tell us?

It is independently supported fact recall. Of the independently supported facts covered by the evaluation, the clustering recognized 95.4%. Recall addresses how many such facts were found; it does not tell us the precision of everything identified as independently supported.
Could I describe that as 95.4% shared-fact accuracy?

That would change the measure. The reported value is 95.4% independently supported fact recall for the clustering. It is not a shared-fact accuracy result for a language model, and it should retain its stated metric name.
Do the two percentages use the same denominator?

Not by virtue of being percentages from the same evaluation. Source-exclusive precision concerns items identified as source-exclusive; independently supported fact recall concerns the independently supported facts to be found. The result gives the two metric values but not their underlying counts or denominators.
Can we calculate the exact numbers of correctly classified claims from the percentages and the 1,200 total?

No. The total of 1,200 claims does not tell us how many items were identified as source-exclusive or how many independently supported facts were in the relevant recall set. Without those counts, converting either percentage into an exact number of claims or facts would be unwarranted.
How should we connect these measurements to the concern about paraphrased overlap?

They provide results for clustering on ParaphraseProvenance-1, the setting used to examine that concern: 96.1% source-exclusive precision and 95.4% independently supported fact recall across the 1,200 claims. The figures do not separately report performance for particular kinds of paraphrase or explain how individual paraphrased claims were grouped.
Does source-exclusive precision tell us whether every exclusive span was located?

No. Precision examines the items identified as exclusive and asks how often that identification was correct. Finding every exclusive span would be a recall question for that category, and no source-exclusive recall value is reported here.
Conversely, does independently supported fact recall tell us whether every fact labeled independently supported truly had independent support?

No. That would concern precision for the independently supported category. The reported 95.4% is recall: how many independently supported facts were recognized. Keeping those directions separate avoids assigning either result a meaning it does not have.
What is the most precise way to report the result without implying more than was measured?

“On 1,200 ParaphraseProvenance-1 claims, clustering achieved 96.1% source-exclusive precision and 95.4% independently supported fact recall.” That gives the setting, sample size, measured values, and metric names without inventing additional outcomes.
Does this result tell us whether gradient ascent removed source-specific information from a model?

No. It reports how the clustering performed on the two stated measures. It does not report applying gradient ascent to a model or measuring extraction of source-exclusive information after unlearning.
Does it establish that original-model distillation preserved independently supported facts in a model?
